generatedBy: SI drafted from NASA's Researcher's Guide to Combustion Science, the challenge statement and the PSI records. Checked by the team.

terms.definition: A flame that burns at a low temperature with little or no visible light. NASA's Researcher's Guide describes stable cool flames that form after the visible flame of a heptane droplet goes out. FLEX discovered this, and CFI and CFI-G studied it further.
The near weightless condition of freefall, as on the International Space Station. Hot gas does not rise, so flames lose the upward flow that feeds them on Earth and often become round.
Gravity between zero and Earth level, such as the Moon at 0.166 g or Mars at 0.38 g. PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion tests yet.
A flame where fuel and oxygen start apart and meet at the flame. A candle is one. Most accidental fires are diffusion flames.
An inside-out flame. The oxidizer flows from the burner into a surrounding fuel gas. In these tests the oxygen value describes the oxidizer stream and not a cabin atmosphere.
A classical result for a burning droplet. The square of its diameter falls in a straight line with time. The slope is the burning rate constant.
How fast the square of a droplet's diameter shrinks, in square millimetres per second. A larger value means the droplet burns away faster.
The point where a flame goes out. In FLEX, extinction means the visible flame went out before the droplet was fully burned.
The boundary between conditions where a material burns and where it does not, for example the lowest oxygen level that still supports a flame.
An atmosphere that gives the same oxygen partial pressure as sea level air, about 0.21 atm. Lower pressure with more oxygen can keep breathing normal and still make materials easier to burn.
An inert gas mixed into the atmosphere or the fuel, such as nitrogen, carbon dioxide or helium. Diluents take heat from a flame and can put it out.

The FLEX record names carbon dioxide and helium among the gaseous fire suppressants it set out to measure. FLEX burned droplets in atmospheres with added carbon dioxide to see how well it suppresses a flame.
Helium carries heat away from a flame quickly. FLEX and CFI used helium in some atmospheres to study extinction and cool flames.
Polymethyl methacrylate, a clear plastic also known as acrylic. It burns steadily, so it is a standard sample in flammability tests such as BASS-II and Saffire-II.
A fabric of 75 percent cotton on a 25 percent fiberglass backing, made for flame spread tests. BASS and Saffire burned it.
Concurrent means the flame spreads in the same direction as the air flow. Opposed means it spreads against the flow. Saffire and BASS tested both.
The flame size at which a flame starts to release soot as smoke. SPICE measured smoke points of gas jet flames in microgravity.
The tiny particles and droplets that make up smoke. Their size decides whether a detector can see them. SAME and SAME-R measured them in microgravity.
The temperature a flame would reach if it lost no heat. It is a calculated upper value. The ACME tables list it in a column headed Tad (K).
EMBER's count of real flight tests near a chosen habitat atmosphere, on a scale of 0 to 100. It is not a safety rating.

The three parts of spacecraft fire safety named in the challenge statement. Prevention is about materials and ignition sources. Detection is about sensing smoke. Suppression is about putting a fire out.
NASA's standard flammability screening test, an upward flame propagation test in normal gravity. BASS and Saffire set out to connect it with real behaviour in microgravity.
A combustion laboratory rack on the ISS. It hosted the droplet experiments FLEX, FLEX-2 and CFI, and the ACME gas flame experiments.
A sealed work volume on the ISS where crew can run small experiments by hand. BASS, BASS-II, SPICE and SLICE ran in it.
An uncrewed supply ship. After it left the ISS, the Saffire experiments burned large samples inside it, which would be too risky with a crew aboard.

A cabin atmosphere with more oxygen at lower pressure than sea level air, planned so crews can start spacewalks faster. NASA reports give 34 percent oxygen at 8.2 psi. The challenge statement expects 30 percent or more at 10.2 psi or less for a Moon Base.
